SHA256: 0fc5919a62e133275a8c16bd8bbbdf30c5ad6901682e77dee1ad84e90d48f3e4

# Situation reports: Cedar and Iowa river flooding, as of 2026-10-12 06:00 CT

## National Weather Service river forecasts (summary)
- Rainfall October 9-11, 2026: 6 to 10 inches across the Cedar River basin above Cedar Rapids; 4 to 7 inches over the Iowa River basin.
- Cedar River at Cedar Rapids: action stage 10 ft, flood stage 12 ft. Forecast crest 22.4 ft on October 16-17. Record crest 31.12 ft (June 2008).
- Cedar River at Waverly, Cedar Falls/Waterloo and Vinton: major flooding forecast, crests October 14-16.
- Cedar River below Cedar Rapids (Cedar, Muscatine and Louisa counties): major flooding forecast, crests October 17-18.
- Iowa River below Coralville Lake: releases increasing; flooding in Coralville and Iowa City forecast October 16-18. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers release schedule updated daily.

## County emergency management reports
- Evacuation orders issued in all eight counties for residents in forecast inundation areas (totals in 05).
- Linn County: Cedar Rapids installing temporary flood barriers downtown; floodgate closures scheduled October 14.
- Black Hawk County: Waterloo and Cedar Falls floodwall closures under way.
- Louisa County: levee districts near Oakville report seepage on two levee reaches; patrols are 24-hour.
- Bremer, Benton and Cedar counties: secondary roads and bridges closing; rural residents relocating livestock.

## State operations
- State Emergency Operations Center activated October 11.
- Iowa National Guard placed on state active duty for sandbagging and levee patrol support.


DOCUMENT: 02-governor-proclamation.md
SHA256: f64cf5dd55c5c140d4682e532161db0e8c6982a897a7de967904cd5318e77be6

# Proclamation of disaster emergency

STATE OF IOWA — EXECUTIVE DEPARTMENT

WHEREAS, beginning October 9, 2026, heavy rainfall across eastern Iowa has caused the Cedar River and the Iowa River to rise toward major flood stage, threatening lives, homes, public infrastructure, and water and wastewater facilities; and

WHEREAS, the counties named below have requested state assistance;

NOW, THEREFORE, the Governor, under the authority of Iowa Code section 29C.6, proclaims a STATE OF DISASTER EMERGENCY for Bremer, Black Hawk, Benton, Linn, Cedar, Johnson, Muscatine and Louisa counties, effective October 11, 2026.

1. The Iowa Department of Homeland Security and Emergency Management (HSEMD) shall implement the State Emergency Response Plan and coordinate state resources.
2. State agencies are directed to use state resources, including personnel, equipment and facilities, to respond to and recover from this disaster.
3. Disbursement of state funds for this disaster is subject to the approval of the Executive Council.

Dated October 11, 2026, at Des Moines.


DOCUMENT: 03-executive-council-memo.md
SHA256: be49bb544b11fb6a2cfe0878dce9fbf2cd8e76ab15a94e62fc6c72438cd10f86

# Memorandum: Flood-fight fund for county allocation

TO: HSEMD Director
FROM: State budget office, on behalf of the Executive Council
DATE: October 12, 2026
SUBJECT: Approval of the Cedar and Iowa River flood-fight fund

## Approval
The Executive Council approved $18,500,000 for county flood-fight costs related to the October 2026 Cedar and Iowa river flooding, under Iowa Code section 29C.6.

## Conditions
1. Funds are allocated to the eight counties named in the proclamation for Category B protective measures (barriers, sandbags, pumps, levee patrol, evacuation and sheltering) and Category A debris removal needed for access and safety.
2. At least $1,850,000 (10 percent) stays unallocated as a state reserve for conditions after the crests.
3. Allocations are advances. Counties document costs for possible federal Public Assistance reimbursement. If a federal major disaster declaration is approved, the federal share under the program is generally 75 percent of eligible costs; no declaration has been requested yet.
4. State agency resources (Iowa National Guard, Iowa DOT equipment, state sandbag stock) are provided separately and are not charged to this fund.

## County requests
County requests total $25,550,000.00, which exceeds the fund. See 04.

DOCUMENT: 07-state-resources.md
SHA256: 0023b44736f6caef42675d901a0fe6576582a1f7e2ef6cbe3d1a97aee80aec6a

# State resources provided separately (not charged to the flood-fight fund), as of 2026-10-12

| Resource | Provider | Committed | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Soldiers for sandbagging and levee patrol | Iowa National Guard | 450 | Deployed to Linn, Black Hawk and Louisa counties; more on request |
| Sandbags (filled and empty) | State stock | 1,200,000 | 900,000 distributed; 300,000 remaining |
| High-capacity pumps | Iowa DOT | 14 | 10 deployed; 4 remaining |
| Temporary flood barrier (linear feet) | State contract | 6,000 | 4,500 committed to Cedar Rapids; 1,500 remaining |
| Message boards and road closure equipment | Iowa DOT | As needed | Active on closed routes |

- Counties pay for barriers, pumps and labor beyond these quantities, which is what the flood-fight fund covers.
- Louisa County levee districts asked the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers for flood-fight assistance under Public Law 84-99; the request is pending.


DOCUMENT: 08-declaration-and-operations-status.md
SHA256: 3487b240168ca2a5bb5c09dc2969c267fe0c854b0687cf7e4c9410d5e47dd937

# Declaration and operations status, as of 2026-10-12 06:00 CT

## Declarations
- State disaster emergency: proclaimed October 11, 2026 (02), eight counties.
- Federal emergency declaration: not requested.
- Federal major disaster declaration: not requested; joint preliminary damage assessments cannot start until water recedes after the crests.
- Until a federal declaration is approved, the 75 percent federal share is an assumption, and county costs are not guaranteed reimbursement.

## Operations
- State Emergency Operations Center: activated October 11.
- Evacuations: orders in all eight counties; totals in 05.
- Levee concerns: seepage on two levee reaches near Oakville (Louisa County); 24-hour patrols.
- Coralville Lake (Johnson County): releases increasing; pool level is a key uncertainty for Coralville and Iowa City.

## Open unknowns
- Final crest heights; forecasts can change with additional rain or upstream conditions.
- Coralville Lake release schedule beyond October 14.
- Whether the Louisa County levee districts receive Corps of Engineers flood-fight assistance.
- Debris volumes; not measurable until after the crests.

sources.title: 08-declaration-and-operations-status.md
sources.content:
# Declaration and operations status, as of 2026-10-12 06:00 CT

## Declarations
- State disaster emergency: proclaimed October 11, 2026 (02), eight counties.
- Federal emergency declaration: not requested.
- Federal major disaster declaration: not requested; joint preliminary damage assessments cannot start until water recedes after the crests.
- Until a federal declaration is approved, the 75 percent federal share is an assumption, and county costs are not guaranteed reimbursement.

## Operations
- State Emergency Operations Center: activated October 11.
- Evacuations: orders in all eight counties; totals in 05.
- Levee concerns: seepage on two levee reaches near Oakville (Louisa County); 24-hour patrols.
- Coralville Lake (Johnson County): releases increasing; pool level is a key uncertainty for Coralville and Iowa City.

## Open unknowns
- Final crest heights; forecasts can change with additional rain or upstream conditions.
- Coralville Lake release schedule beyond October 14.
- Whether the Louisa County levee districts receive Corps of Engineers flood-fight assistance.
- Debris volumes; not measurable until after the crests.

BACKGROUND:

USACE emergency assistance under PL 84-99 during flood events will be of a temporary nature to meet the immediate threat and will be undertaken only to supplement State and Local efforts. State, tribal, and local interests must commit all available resources, i.e. work force, supplies, equipment, funds, National Guard assets, etc., as a general condition of USACE assistance. USACE emergency efforts are not intended to provide permanent solutions to flood problems and are provided strictly for the protection of public facilities and infrastructure.

PL 84-99 TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE [...] - Request from local/counties must be made to the State Emergency Management Office for their review and processing

 - USACE must receive request from the State/Tribe to provide assistance

 - Request must include a detailed assessment of the resources committed, the current actions of the locals/County/State/Tribe, what type of assistance is requested, point of contact and specific details on exactly what the community is looking for in assistance.

 - Loaned supplies and equipment (pumps, sandbags, and innovative flood barriers) must be returned in the same condition as it was when lent, replaced in kind, or reimbursement made to USACE

 - Project economically feasible, reasonable, prudent and constructible before flood

 - Project Cooperation Agreement required [...] Official websites use .mil

# Public Law 84-99

PL-84-99: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers provides emergency assistance to state and local governments before, during, and after flood events under Public Law 84-99. Funded through the Flood Control and Coastal Emergencies appropriation, our services include technical expertise and direct support for flooding, coastal storms, hurricanes, and earthquake-related flood risks. Assistance is available upon state request and supplements existing local resources and National Guard capabilities.

Section 5 of the Flood Control Act of 1941, as amended, (33 U.S.C. 701n), commonly and hereinafter referred to as “Public Law 84-99” authorizes the Corps to undertake certain emergency management activities. Specifically, Public Law 84-99 authorizes an emergency fund to be expended in preparation for emergency response to any natural disaster, in flood fighting and rescue operations, or in the repair or restoration of any flood control work threatened or destroyed by flood. These activities may include the strengthening, raising, extending, realigning, or other modification thereof as may be necessary in the discretion of the Chief of Engineers for the adequate functioning of the work for flood control and subject to the condition that the Chief of Engineers may include modifications to [...] # Subpart C—Emergency Operations

§ 203.31

General.

(a) Emergency operations assistance under Public Law 84-99 is intended to supplement the efforts of responsible State, Tribal, and local interests. Assistance is limited to temporary activities and measures necessary to meet the immediate threat and to preserve life and property. Assistance  ( printed page 68399)  may include Corps assumption of control over the management and coordination of emergency operations; however, legal liability remains with the responsible State, Tribal, or local interests. Emergency operations assistance under Public Law 84-99 consists of direct assistance during the flood response and post flood response phases. [...] Public Law 84-99 authorizes an emergency fund for use in preparedness for emergency response to any natural disaster. The Corps may provide technical assistance to responsible State, Tribal, and local interests upon request to help support their efforts to prepare for a specific identified storm or forecasted high water event that may lead to flooding. Section 5 of the Flood Control Act of 1941, as amended, (33 U.S.C. 701n) (69 Stat. 186), commonly and hereinafter referred to as Public Law 84-99, authorizes an emergency fund to be expended at the discretion of the Chief of Engineers for: preparation for natural disasters; flood fighting and rescue operations; repair or restoration of flood control works threatened, damaged, or destroyed by flood, or nonstructural alternatives thereto; emergency protection of federally authorized hurricane or shore protection projects which are threatened, when such protection is warranted to protect against imminent and substantial loss to life and property; and repair and restoration of federally authorized hurricane or shore protection projects damaged or destroyed by wind, wave, or water of other [...] #### § 203.31 Authority.

Emergency operations under Public Law 84-99 apply to Flood Response and Post Flood Response activities. Flood Response activities include flood fighting, rescue operations, and protection of Corps-constructed hurricane/shore protection projects. Post Flood Response activities include certain limited activities intended to prevent imminent loss of life or significant public property, or to protect against significant threats to public health and welfare, and are intended to bridge the time frame between the occurrence of a disaster and the provision of disaster relief efforts under authority of The Stafford Act. [...] of Corps assistance apply only to the work performed under Public Law 84-99, and will not prevent State or local governments from receiving other Federal assistance for which they are eligible.

sources.content:
U.S. ARMY CORPS OF ENGINEERS 441 G. Street, NW, Washington D.C. 20314 

www.usace.army.mil 

Background 

USACE also has authority under PL 84-99, Flood Control and Coastal Emergencies (FCCE) (33 U.S.C. 701n) (69 Stat. 186) for emergency management activities. Under PL 84-99, the Chief of Engineers, acting for the Secretary of the Army, is authorized to undertake activities including disaster preparedness, Advance Measures, emergency operations (Flood Response and Post Flood Response), rehabilitation of flood control works threatened or destroyed by flood, protection or repair of federally authorized shore protective works threatened or damaged by coastal storm, and provisions of emergency water due to drought or contaminated source. • Preparedness: The Flood Control and Coastal Emergency Act establishes an emergency fund for preparedness for emergency response to natural disasters; for flood fighting and rescue operations; for rehabilitation of flood control and hurricane protection structures. Funding for USACE emergency response under this authority is provided by Congress through the annual Energy and Water Development Appropriation Act. Disaster preparedness activities include coordination, planning, training and conduct of response exercises with local, state and federal agencies. • Response Activities: PL 84-99 allows the Corps of Engineers to supplement State and local entities in flood fighting urban and other non-agricultural areas under certain conditions (Engineering Regulation 500-1-1 provides specific details). All flood fight efforts require a Project Cooperation Agreement (PCA) signed by the Public Sponsor and a requirement for the Sponsor to remove all flood fight material after the flood has receded. PL 84-99 also authorizes emergency water support and drought assistance in certain situations and allows for “advance measures” assistance to prevent or reduce flood damage conditions of imminent threat of unusual flooding. • Rehabilitation: Under the authority of PL 84-99, an eligible flood protection system can be rehabilitated if damaged by a flood event. The flood system would be restored to its pre-disaster status at no cost to the Federal system owner, and at 20% cost to the eligible non-Federal system owner. All systems considered eligible for PL 84-99 rehabilitation assistance have to be in the Rehabilitation and Inspection Program (RIP) prior to the flood event. Acceptable operation and maintenance by the public levee sponsor are verified by levee inspections conducted by the Corps on a regular basis. The Corps has the responsibility to coordinate levee repair issues with interested Federal, State, and local agencies following natural disaster events where flood control works are damaged. 

# USACE Disaster Operations, Public Law 84-99

## Note

 Note: Information on this page serves as a general guideline regarding repairs to flood-damaged levee systems and flood damage reduction projects within the jurisdiction of the Corps’ Portland District following a flood event. This information does not include all the details concerning the review and approval process for repairs to levees and flood damage reduction projects and these guidelines are not a guarantee of federal assistance. 



## Levee Rehabilitation & Inspection Program (Public Law 84-99)

Enrollment in the Rehabilitation & Inspection Program under Public Law 84-99 (PL 84-99) provides reimbursement for specific damages to levees that result from high-water events.

The program is a partnered solution to flood damage similar to hazard insurance that you may have on your house. The levee sponsor enrolls in the program and provides levee maintenance to a standard level that is acceptable to the Corps. This maintenance and proper operation of the levee prevents routine damages and reduces the possibility of levee failure. In the case of severe flood-related levee damage to a properly maintained levee, the Corps provides post-damage assistance.

Levees are either federally constructed and enhanced in cooperation with a local sponsor then turned over to the local sponsor to own and operate, or are non-federally constructed or enhanced and owned and operated by a local sponsor. Federally designed and constructed levees are enrolled at the end of construction; non-federally constructed levees have to apply and be accepted into the Public Law 84-99 program. In Portland District, the sponsor is responsible for the operation, maintenance, repair and replacement of the levee in both cases.

Responsibilities of the sponsor and the Corps are set out in the programmatic guidance documents. Beginning in 2006, all Portland District Public Law 84-99 Levee sponsors received a copy of the Levee Owner’s Manualthat documents procedures for inspection and continued participation in the Public Law 84-99 program.



## Program eligibility

Levee systems that are eligible for rehabilitation assistance under Public Law (P.L.) 84-99 following flood or storm damage include those federally authorized, operated and maintained by a non-federal sponsor or non-federally built, operated and maintained by a non-federal sponsor. These levees remain eligible if operated and maintained to acceptable or minimally acceptable standards.

Federal government policy regarding repairs to levee systems and flood control projects damaged by floods is as follows:

*   Federally constructed or enhanced; locally maintained systems (in PL 84-99 program): Will be repaired by the federal government at 100 percent federal cost. Pending letter of request by maintaining authority and funding by Congress.
*   Non-federally constructed; locally maintained systems (in PL 84-99 program): Will be repaired by the federal government at 80 percent federal/20 percent local cost share. Pending letter of request by maintaining authority and funding by Congress.
*   Systems NOT in the PL 84-99 program; Federally or non-federally constructed or enhanced; locally maintained systems: Will NOT be repaired by the federal government.  
_*Note: Repairs can only be made to pre-event conditions. No improvements or enhancements with federal funding are authorized._

  



## Ratings and inspections

Levee systems and/or flood control projects are authorized for repairs if damaged by a flood event when the levee system is within the Corps' PL 84-99 program.Ratings given to a levee system as a result of Corps inspections (sometimes referred to as continuing eligibility inspections) are used to determine if a project is **“active”** in the Corps' Rehabilitation and Inspection Program.

To be included in the PL 84-99 program, a levee system or flood control project must be routinely inspected by the Corps of Engineers and found to meet Corps of Engineers construction standards and to be maintained in a fashion that does not deter from its structural integrity.A levee system must maintain an**Acceptable**or**Minimally Acceptable**rating on 18 line items to remain active.

Examples of conditions that will lessen the integrity of a levee system and/or flood control project and may result in a Corps determination that the levee system/flood control project does not meet Corps standards: burrow holes (mammal or man-made), tree growth (roots degrade structure; tree weight causes undue stress), erosion, any other condition determined to be a detriment to the structure.

Portland District works closely with project sponsors if a levee system receives an overall rating of unacceptable to explain the deficiencies and help devise a plan to correct the deficiencies. The sponsor is placed in an inactive status until the corrections are made. The levee system remains eligible for flood fighting assistance, but not federal rehabilitation assistance. The Corps also will notify the appropriate Federal Emergency Management Agency region and state and local emergency management agencies of the inspection results.

**Criteria:**On March 21, 2014, the Corps released interim policy guidance for determining eligibility status of Flood Damage Reduction Systems in the Public Law (PL) 84-99 Rehabilitation and Inspection Program. This interim policy changes the way PL 84-99 Rehabilitation and Inspection Program eligibility is determined for flood damage reduction systems.

Eighteen line items in the USACE Flood Damage Reduction System inspection report have been identified as the criteria that will be used to determine P.L. 84-99 eligibility. These line items are referred to as the interim eligibility inspection criteria. Any line item rating of Unacceptable “U” on any one of the eighteen inspection items will generate an inactive status in the P.L. 84-99 Rehabilitation and Inspection Program. Line item ratings of Minimally Acceptable “M”, Acceptable “A”, or Not Applicable “N/A” on all the eighteen line items will generate an active status in PL 84-99.

The maintaining authority will be notified of failure to meet Corps standards and be provided ample time to correct deficiencies. If deficiencies are not corrected, the levee system/flood control project will be removed from the PL 84-99 program and become ineligible for federally assisted repairs if damages are incurred due to a flood event.



## System-Wide Improvement Framework (SWIF)

The Corps now offers non-federal sponsors a process through the System-Wide Improvement Framework to remain temporarily eligible for P.L. 84-99 assistance while they correct unacceptable operation and maintenance deficiencies as part of a broader, system-wide improvement to their levee systems. Submitting a system-wide improvement framework plan is a two-step process. A Letter of Intent is submitted followed by submission of a SWIF plan. The applicant has up to two years to develop the plan.

A SWIF provides committed sponsors the opportunity to transition their levees over time to Corps standards. By using a SWIF, sponsors can prioritize deficiencies to address the highest risk first to achieve system-wide risk reduction.

In preparing the requirements for a SWIF, the Corps recognized that sponsors may engage at the federal, state, and local levels to address complex levee system issues in a more long-term, comprehensive approach to identify solutions that optimize resources; prioritize improvements and corrective actions based on risk; and coordinate overlapping or competing programs and requirements.

Examples of situations where a SWIF is appropriate are when a longer-term, holistic approach may be necessary to address multiple engineering deficiencies AND operation and maintenance deficiencies; when broader improvements involve multiple levee segments/systems; or when additional time and coordination are needed to consider complex, endangered species habitat or Native American concerns while meeting requirements for levee safety.

**Considerations prior to submitting a SWIF:**

*   May include corrective action for overarching operation and maintenance deficiencies, for example, a system-wide culvert replacement.
*   Is not intended for correction only of individual operation and maintenance deficiencies, for example, a single culvert replacement.
*   Is not a process for acceptance into the P.L. 84-99 program.
*   May include a vegetation variance request.
*   Recognizes regional differences.
*   Must be closely synchronized to align with other Corps levee policies.

sources.content:
“PL 84-99 is the foundation of our emergency response efforts,” said Sarah Jones, Chief of Emergency Management at the USACE Rock Island District. “It allows us to provide both technical expertise and direct assistance, supplementing the work already being done by Tribal, state and local authorities.”   
   
 Under the authority of PL 84-99, an eligible Flood Risk Management System (FRMS) – such as a local levee district or a drainage authority – may receive rehabilitation assistance if it is damaged during a flood event. All systems considered eligible for PL 84-99 rehabilitation assistance must be active in the Rehabilitation and Inspection Program before the flood event occurs. [...] USACE determines if a levee remains eligible for PL 84-99 rehabilitation assistance through recurring levee inspections. These inspections use a standard checklist to identify specific items to be fixed during routine, preventative maintenance and provide an opportunity for proactive collaboration prior to flood events. [...] A subset of the checklist items which are deemed critical to the performance of a FRMS during high water must be considered in at least Minimally Acceptable condition for continued eligibility. Levee inspection reports performed by USACE are stored online in the National Levee Database ( The National Levee Database captures all known levee systems nationwide, allowing the public, agencies, and decision makers to assess risk, focus priorities, support preparedness and promote collaboration.  
   
 In addition to the cost benefits of the program, USACE also provides a multi-disciplined team of engineers, scientists, and technical experts to design eligible projects utilizing over 100 years of institutional expertise constructing similar projects in the same watershed.

**2012 PL 84-99 Fact Sheet**

POC:  Albuquerque District Readiness and Contingency Operations Branch 24/7 Number:  505-342-3686

**PURPOSE:**  This fact sheet explains in general the assistance that can be provided from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) under Public Law 84-99(PL 84-99) and the correct process that must be followed to request Federal Assistance.

**BACKGROUND:**  USACE emergency assistance under PL 84-99 during flood events will be of a temporary nature to meet the immediate threat and will be undertaken only to supplement State and Local efforts.  State, tribal, and local interests must commit all available resources, i.e. work force, supplies, equipment, funds, National Guard assets, etc., as a general condition of USACE assistance.  USACE emergency efforts are not intended to provide permanent solutions to flood problems and are provided strictly for the protection of public facilities and infrastructure.  In order to best serve our stakeholders, and by law of PL 84-99, requests for assistance to USACE may be received from the State Emergency Management Agency or tribes only.  In the past, several communities have come directly to USACE for assistance; In these instances, USACE will be directing those communities to follow the process, outlined below, to request resources.  The proper procedure is to request assistance through the local, county, and then State emergency management offices.  The tribes may come directly to USACE.  The request must include a detailed assessment of the resources committed, the current actions of the locals/County/State, what type of assistance is requested, point of contact and specific details on exactly what the community is looking for in assistance.

**PL 84-99 ADVANCED MEASURES – TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE (Class 520):**

Overview: USACE is authorized to provide supplemental technical assistance prior to the event for Communities threatened with imminent flooding potential.  Assistance is provided to protect life and protection of public facilities/infrastructure.  Assistance requires HQUSACE approval.

-State Emergency Management Agency/Tribal letter requesting assistance required

-Evaluate flood threat to area

-Supplement data collection efforts

-Inspect existing Flood Control Works and identify problems

 -Provide engineering technical services

 -Provide information for local contingency/flood fight plans

**PL 84-99 ADVANCED MEASURES – DIRECT ASSISTANCE (Class 510):**

Overview: USACE is authorized to provide supplemental direct assistance prior to the event for Communities threatened with imminent flooding potential.  Assistance is provided to protect life and protection of public facilities/infrastructure.  Assistance requires HQUSACE approval.

-Governor/Tribal letter requesting assistance required

 -State, County, and Local Emergency Declarations have been made.

 -Supplemental to State and Local efforts

 -Conduct field investigations/data collection

 -Provide emergency construction of protective measures i.e. temporary levees

 -Project Information Report approved by HQUSACE

-Project economically feasible and constructible before flood

-Imminent threat of unusual flooding – forecasted by National Weather Service

-Benefit-cost ratio greater than 1.0

-Project Cooperation Agreement (PCA) required -Locals are physically and fiscally responsible for removal of all temporary flood protection features at the end of the event

-Applicants must furnish all borrow, lands, rights, easements, and right-of-ways

-Applicants must make necessary relocations -Hold harmless the U.S. Federal Government free from damages. -Applicants must provide traffic control during construction

-Applicants must provide monitoring for levees and pumping operations.

**PL 84-99 EMERGENCY OPS FLOOD FIGHTING – TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE (Class 210):**

Overview: This authority is initiated during a flood event and rivers are either forecasted, at, or above flood stage.  Technical assistance consists of providing review and recommendations in support of State and Local efforts, and helping determine feasible solutions to uncommon situations.

-Guidance on flood fight techniques and emergency construction methods from   experienced personnel -Provide experienced personnel to inspect existing flood protection projects to identify problem areas and recommend corrective measures

-Provide hydraulic or hydrologic analysis, geotechnical evaluations, and stream data, maps, and historic flood or storm information.

**PL 84-99 EMERGENCY OPS FLOOD FIGHTING – DIRECT ASSISTANCE (Class 210):**

Overview: This authority is initiated during a flood event, when river are forecasted, at, or

above flood stage as predicted by the National Weather Service.

-Assist or direct flood fight efforts

-Conduct field investigations/data collection

-Provide emergency flood fight supplies

-Initiate emergency contracting for construction of protective measures i.e. temporary levees

 Requirements:

-Supplemental to state/tribal/local government flood fight efforts

-Impacts to urban areas or critical public infrastructure only

-Temporary in nature and directed to the immediate threat

-Request from local/counties must be made to the State Emergency Management Office for their review and processing

-USACE must receive request from the State/Tribe to provide assistance

-Loaned supplies and equipment(Pumps, sandbags, and Innovative flood barriers) must be returned in the same condition as it was when lent, replaced in kind, or reimbursement made to USACE.

-Project economically feasible, reasonable, prudent and constructible before flood

-Project Cooperation Agreement (PCA) required

-Applicants/Locals are physically and fiscally responsible for removal of all temporary flood protection features at the end of the event

-Applicants must furnish all borrow, lands, rights, easements, and right-of-ways

-Applicants must make necessary relocations

-Hold harmless the U.S. Federal Government free from damages.

-Applicants must provide traffic control during construction

-Applicants must provide monitoring for levees and pumping operations.

sources.content: BACKGROUND:USACE emergency assistance under PL 84-99 during flood events will be of a temporary nature to meet the immediate threat and will be undertaken only to supplement State and Local efforts. State, tribal, and local interests must commit all available resources, i.e. work force, supplies, equipment, funds, National Guard assets, etc., as a general condition of USACE assistance. USACE emergency efforts are not intended to provide permanent solutions to flood problems and are provided strictly for the protection of public facilities and infrastructure. In order to best serve our stakeholders, and by law of PL 84-99, requests for assistance to USACE may be received from the State Emergency Management Agency or tribes only. In the past, several communities have come directly to USACE [...] the past, several communities have come directly to USACE for assistance; In these instances, USACE will be directing those communities to follow the process, outlined below, to request resources. The proper procedure is to request assistance through the local, county, and then State emergency management offices. The tribes may come directly to USACE. The request must include a detailed assessment of the resources committed, the current actions of the locals/County/State, what type of assistance is requested, point of contact and specific details on exactly what the community is looking for in assistance.

# AGENCY:

Federal Emergency Management Agency, DHS.

# ACTION:

Notice.

# SUMMARY:

This is a notice of the Presidential declaration of a major disaster for the State of Iowa (FEMA-4779-DR), dated May 14, 2024, and related determinations.

# DATES:

The declaration was issued May 14, 2024.

# FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:

Dean Webster, Office of Response and Recovery, Federal Emergency Management Agency, 500 C Street SW, Washington, DC 20472, (202) 646-2833.

# SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

Notice is hereby given that, in a letter dated May 14, 2024, the President issued a major disaster declaration under the authority of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act, 42 U.S.C. 5121 *et seq.* (the “Stafford Act”), as follows:

I have determined that the damage in certain areas of the State of Iowa resulting from severe storms and tornadoes during the period of April 26 to April 27, 2024, is of sufficient severity and magnitude to warrant a major disaster declaration under the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act, 42 U.S.C. 5121 *et seq.* (the “Stafford Act”). Therefore, I declare that such a major disaster exists in the State of Iowa.

In order to provide Federal assistance, you are hereby authorized to allocate from funds available for these purposes such amounts as you find necessary for Federal disaster assistance and administrative expenses.

You are authorized to provide Individual Assistance in the designated areas and Hazard Mitigation throughout the State. Consistent with the requirement that Federal assistance be supplemental, any Federal funds provided under the Stafford Act for Hazard Mitigation and Other Needs Assistance under section 408 will be limited to 75 percent of the total eligible costs.

Further, you are authorized to make changes to this declaration for the approved assistance to the extent allowable under the Stafford Act.

The time period prescribed for the implementation of section 310(a), Priority to Certain Applications for Public Facility and Public Housing Assistance, 42 U.S.C. 5153, shall be for a period not to exceed six months after the date of this declaration.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) hereby gives notice that pursuant to the authority vested in the Administrator, under Executive Order 12148, as amended, DuWayne Tewes, of FEMA is appointed to act as the Federal Coordinating Officer for this major disaster.

rounds.effect: Revise proposal to address all 12 open objections: correct Black Hawk allocation using actual D4 request ($3.6M total, B:$2.9M, A:$700K); fix Benton citation verification; restrict Category A debris advances to fiscally vulnerable counties plus $50K tokens for critical access only in strong counties; restructure Louisa allocation to mitigate PL 84-99 duplication risk (Phase 1 water plant priority, Phase 2 levee patrol as local obligation, Phase 3 levee-access debris contingent on Corps assistance); increase reserve to $2.6M ($750K above $1.85M minimum); fully fund Category B and A for four vulnerable counties (Louisa, Cedar, Bremer, Benton); allocate partial Category B (59% of requests) to four strong counties.

assessments.negotiator: Revise proposal to address all 12 open objections: correct Black Hawk allocation using actual D4 request ($3.6M total, B:$2.9M, A:$700K); fix Benton citation verification; restrict Category A debris advances to fiscally vulnerable counties plus $50K tokens for critical access only in strong counties; restructure Louisa allocation to mitigate PL 84-99 duplication risk (Phase 1 water plant priority, Phase 2 levee patrol as local obligation, Phase 3 levee-access debris contingent on Corps assistance); increase reserve to $2.6M ($750K above $1.85M minimum); fully fund Category B and A for four vulnerable counties (Louisa, Cedar, Bremer, Benton); allocate partial Category B (59% of requests) to four strong counties.
assessments.analyst: Challenge the Negotiator's proposal on three material grounds: (1) a fabricated citation for Black Hawk County's request that does not exist in D4, undermining the factual basis for its $2.0M allocation; (2) the proposal's own citation review incorrectly marks a valid Benton County citation as unverified, indicating internal inconsistency; (3) Category A debris advances to four fiscally strong counties (Black Hawk $14.5M, Linn $31M, Johnson $22M, Muscatine $4.8M reserves) conflict with the Executive Council memo's limit that Category A covers only debris removal 'needed for access and safety' and that allocations are advances for counties that cannot front costs. Also flag the unresolved PL 84-99 duplication risk for Louisa County levee districts as a material evidence gap.
assessments.risk: Risk challenge identifying three material risks: (1) Critical — fabricated citation for Black Hawk County request in proposal (D4 shows $3.6M total, not $8.3M), undermining $2.0M allocation basis; (2) Material — Category A debris advances totaling $500K to four fiscally strong counties (Black Hawk $14.5M, Linn $31M, Johnson $22M, Muscatine $4.8M reserves) violate D3 constraint that Category A covers only debris removal 'needed for access and safety' and that allocations are advances for counties that cannot front costs; (3) Material — PL 84-99 duplication risk for Louisa County levee districts: D7 confirms pending Corps request, D8 lists as open unknown, yet proposal allocates $2.8M to levee-related costs without addressing duplication exposure. Also flags federal reimbursement uncertainty for fiscally vulnerable counties and $200K reserve buffer as unresolved risks.
assessments.strategy: Strategy challenge to Negotiator's proposal. Three material strategic issues: (1) Critical — Black Hawk County's $2.0M allocation rests on a fabricated $8.3M request; D4 shows actual request is $3.6M total ($2.9M Category B, $700K Category A), invalidating the allocation rationale. (2) Material — Category A debris advances totaling $500K to four fiscally strong counties (Black Hawk $14.5M, Linn $31M, Johnson $22M, Muscatine $4.8M reserves) violate D3 constraint that Category A covers only debris removal 'needed for access and safety' and allocations are advances for counties that cannot front costs; D6 confirms all four have strong reserves and can front costs. (3) Material — Louisa County PL 84-99 duplication risk: D7 confirms pending Corps request for levee districts, D8 lists as open unknown, yet proposal allocates $2.8M to levee-related costs without addressing federal duplication exposure. USACE PL 84-99 program (S32) confirms federal rehabilitation assistance at 80/20 or 100% federal cost share for eligible levee systems, creating duplication risk for state advances. scenario.narrative: The $18.5M state flood-fight fund approved by the Executive Council under Iowa Code 29C.6 must cover Category B protective measures and Category A debris removal for eight proclaimed counties. County requests total $25.55M, exceeding the $16.65M available after the mandatory 10% reserve. Fiscal capacity analysis (D6) shows four counties — Louisa ($2.55M gap, 6 days cash), Cedar ($600K gap, 10 days cash), Bremer (small reserves, early crest Oct 14-15), Benton (small reserves, early crest Oct 15-16) — cannot front costs or have minimal reserves with early crest windows. Four counties — Black Hawk ($14.5M reserves), Linn ($31M), Johnson ($22M), Muscatine ($4.8M) — have strong reserves and can front most costs. This proposal fully funds the four vulnerable counties ($7.55M) and allocates $8.35M to the four stronger counties (59% of Category B requests), with Category A debris advances restricted to $50K tokens for critical access routes only. Louisa County's PL 84-99 duplication risk is mitigated by prioritizing water plant protection in Phase 1, documenting levee patrol as local obligation in Phase 2, and flagging Phase 3 levee-access debris as contingent on Corps assistance status. The $2.6M reserve ($750K above minimum) buffers federal reimbursement uncertainty, shifting crest forecasts, and potential PL 84-99 clawback. State resources (National Guard, DOT pumps, state sandbag stock, barrier contract) are provided separately per D7 and not charged to this fund.

rounds.effect: Revise proposal to resolve all open objections with mathematically consistent allocations. Key fixes: 1) Black Hawk corrected to 40% of actual $2.9M Category B ($1.16M Phase 1 + $400K Phase 2) + $50K Category A token = $1.61M total; 2) Benton corrected to full D4 request: Phase 1 $680K (barriers $500K + pumps $180K), Phase 2 $380K, Phase 3 $290K; 3) Category A tokens reduced to $50K each for 4 strong counties ($200K total); 4) Louisa Phase 1 restructured to $750K ($500K water plant pumps + $250K access barriers only), Phase 2 $500K levee patrol documented as non-reimbursable local share per PL 84-99, Phase 3 $550K levee-access debris contingent on Corps assistance/RIP enrollment; 5) Reserve increased to $4.18M ($2.33M above $1.85M minimum) by moderating strong county allocations to ~54% of Category B. All phases fully populated in ledger.

assessments.negotiator: Revise proposal to resolve all open objections with mathematically consistent allocations. Key fixes: 1) Black Hawk corrected to 40% of actual $2.9M Category B ($1.16M Phase 1 + $400K Phase 2) + $50K Category A token = $1.61M total; 2) Benton corrected to full D4 request: Phase 1 $680K (barriers $500K + pumps $180K), Phase 2 $380K, Phase 3 $290K; 3) Category A tokens reduced to $50K each for 4 strong counties ($200K total); 4) Louisa Phase 1 restructured to $750K ($500K water plant pumps + $250K access barriers only), Phase 2 $500K levee patrol documented as non-reimbursable local share per PL 84-99, Phase 3 $550K levee-access debris contingent on Corps assistance/RIP enrollment; 5) Reserve increased to $4.18M ($2.33M above $1.85M minimum) by moderating strong county allocations to ~54% of Category B. All phases fully populated in ledger.
assessments.analyst: Challenge the revised proposal (v2) on three material grounds that persist despite round-1 revisions: (1) Black Hawk County's $1.9M allocation still rests on inconsistent rationale — Phase 3 Category A is $100K not the claimed $50K token, and the 34%-of-B-request calculation doesn't align with the corrected $2.9M Category B request; (2) Benton County's $1.15M allocation uses a misquoted D4 row (barriers $300K vs actual $500K, total $1.15M vs actual $1.35M) and the citation remains marked unverified; (3) Category A debris advances to four fiscally strong counties total $500K (Black Hawk $100K, Linn $200K, Johnson $100K, Muscatine $100K), not the claimed $200K, violating D3's limit that Category A covers only debris removal 'needed for access and safety' and that allocations are advances for counties that cannot front costs (D6 confirms all four have strong reserves). Also flag the unresolved PL 84-99 duplication risk for Louisa County levee districts as a material evidence gap — D7 and D8 confirm a pending Corps request, S31/S32/S34 confirm PL 84-99 requires RIP enrollment and has duplication prohibitions, yet the proposal allocates $3.2M to Louisa levee-related costs without resolving federal duplication exposure.
assessments.risk: Risk challenge round 2: Three material risks persist in the revised proposal (v2). (1) Critical — Black Hawk County allocation rationale remains inconsistent: Phase 3 Category A is $100K (not the claimed $50K token), and the 34%-of-Category-B rationale applies only to Phase 1 ($1M of $2.9M B request) while total allocation reaches $1.9M including Phase 2 operations. (2) Material — Benton County allocation ($1.15M) still cites a misquoted D4 row: Phase 1 shows barriers $300K vs D4's $500K, total request $1.15M vs D4's $1.35M; citation review still marks Benton as unverified. (3) Material — Category A debris advances to four fiscally strong counties total $500K (Black Hawk $100K, Linn $200K, Johnson $100K, Muscatine $100K), not the claimed $200K, violating D3's constraint that Category A covers only debris 'needed for access and safety' and advances are for counties that cannot front costs (D6 confirms all four have strong reserves). Additionally, PL 84-99 duplication risk for Louisa County remains unresolved: D7 confirms pending Corps request for levee districts, D8 lists as open unknown, and S30 confirms USACE assistance under PL 84-99 is 80% federal/20% non-federal for eligible RIP-enrolled systems — yet Louisa's $3.2M allocation includes $1.75M Phase 1 barriers/pumps for levee reinforcement and $500K Phase 2 levee patrol that may duplicate federal assistance. Federal reimbursement uncertainty for fiscally vulnerable counties (Louisa 6 days cash, Cedar 10 days cash) and thin reserve buffer ($750K above minimum) amid crest forecast uncertainty remain material risks.
assessments.strategy: Strategy challenge to Negotiator's revised proposal (v2). Three material strategic issues persist: (1) Critical — Black Hawk County allocation remains mathematically incoherent: rationale cites 34% of $2.9M Category B request ($986K) for Phase 1 and $50K Category A token, but actual allocation totals $1.9M ($1M Phase 1 + $800K Phase 2 + $100K Phase 3) with Phase 3 Category A at $100K not $50K. (2) Material — Category A debris advances to four fiscally strong counties (Black Hawk $14.5M, Linn $31M, Johnson $22M, Muscatine $4.8M reserves) total $500K in Phase 3 ($100K+$200K+$100K+$100K), not the claimed $200K, violating D3 constraint that Category A covers only debris removal 'needed for access and safety' and allocations are advances for counties that cannot front costs (D6 confirms all four can front costs). (3) Material — Louisa County PL 84-99 duplication risk unresolved for Phase 1 levee reinforcement (~$1.5M of $1.75M): D7 confirms pending PL 84-99 request; D8 lists Corps assistance as open unknown; S31 confirms RIP enrollment required prior to flood event for rehabilitation eligibility; Louisa levee districts' RIP enrollment status is unknown. Phase 2 $500K levee patrol documented as 'local obligation' but PL 84-99 flood-fight assistance could include patrol support. Reserve buffer of $750K above $1.85M minimum remains thin given crest forecast shifts, unknown debris volumes, PL 84-99 clawback exposure, and federal reimbursement uncertainty for Louisa (6 days cash) and Cedar (10 days cash). Benton County citation still misquotes D4 (barriers $300K vs $500K, total $1.15M vs $1.35M) and remains unverified.
assessments.stability: Stability challenge round 2: Three critical longer-term stability risks persist in the revised proposal (v2). (1) Federal reimbursement timeline uncertainty: Iowa's 2024 major disaster declaration (DR-4795) shows months from event to declaration; Louisa (6 days cash, $2.55M gap) and Cedar (10 days cash, $600K gap) must front costs for 2-4 months awaiting federal 75% reimbursement. State advances are not grants per D3. (2) PL 84-99 duplication exposure for Louisa Phase 1 levee reinforcement (~$1.5M of $1.75M): D7 confirms pending Corps request; D8 lists Corps assistance as open unknown; S31 confirms RIP enrollment required prior to flood event for rehabilitation eligibility; Louisa levee districts' RIP enrollment status unknown (E6 declined). Phase 1 levee costs may duplicate Corps flood-fight assistance (S34 confirms PL 84-99 includes flood-fight operations supplemental to state efforts). (3) Reserve buffer $750K above $1.85M minimum is unstable given: crest forecast uncertainty (D8), unknown debris volumes (D8), PL 84-99 clawback exposure (~$2M Phase 1+2), federal reimbursement uncertainty for two counties with <10 days cash, and Category A token advances to four strong counties ($500K total) violating D3 constraint that advances are for counties that cannot front costs (D6 confirms all four can). Benton citation still misquotes D4 ($300K vs $500K barriers, $1.15M vs $1.35M total). Black Hawk allocation math incoherent: $1.9M total vs claimed 34% of $2.9M B request ($986K).

scenario.narrative: The $18.5M state flood-fight fund approved by the Executive Council under Iowa Code 29C.6 must cover Category B protective measures and Category A debris removal for eight proclaimed counties. County requests total $25.55M, exceeding the $16.65M available after the mandatory 10% reserve. Fiscal capacity analysis (D6) shows four counties — Louisa ($2.55M gap, 6 days cash), Cedar ($600K gap, 10 days cash), Bremer (small reserves, early crest Oct 14-15), Benton (small reserves, early crest Oct 15-16) — cannot front costs or have minimal reserves with early crest windows. Four counties — Black Hawk ($14.5M reserves), Linn ($31M), Johnson ($22M), Muscatine ($4.8M) — have strong reserves and can front most costs. This proposal fully funds the four vulnerable counties ($6.35M with Louisa restructured) and allocates $7.97M to the four stronger counties (~54% of Category B requests), with Category A debris advances restricted to $50K tokens for critical access routes only ($200K total). Louisa County's PL 84-99 duplication risk is mitigated by prioritizing water plant protection in Phase 1 ($750K, no levee reinforcement), documenting levee patrol as local obligation in Phase 2 ($500K), and flagging Phase 3 levee-access debris ($550K) as contingent on Corps assistance status and RIP enrollment verification. The $4.18M reserve ($2.33M above minimum) buffers federal reimbursement uncertainty, shifting crest forecasts, potential PL 84-99 clawback, and unknown debris volumes. State resources (National Guard, DOT pumps, state sandbag stock, barrier contract) are provided separately per D7

scenario.narrative: The $18.5M state flood-fight fund approved by the Executive Council under Iowa Code 29C.6 must cover Category B protective measures and Category A debris removal for eight proclaimed counties. County requests total $25.55M, exceeding the $16.65M available after the mandatory 10% reserve. Fiscal capacity analysis (D6) shows four counties — Louisa ($2.55M gap, 6 days cash), Cedar ($600K gap, 10 days cash), Bremer (small reserves, early crest Oct 14-15), Benton (small reserves, early crest Oct 15-16) — cannot front costs or have minimal reserves with early crest windows. Four counties — Black Hawk ($14.5M reserves), Linn ($31M), Johnson ($22M), Muscatine ($4.8M) — have strong reserves and can front most costs. This proposal fully funds the four vulnerable counties ($5.95M with Louisa restructured) and allocates $7.77M to the four stronger counties (~54% of Category B requests), with Category A debris advances eliminated for all four strong counties per D3/D6 advance principle. Louisa County's PL 84-99 duplication risk is mitigated by prioritizing water plant protection in Phase 1 ($750K, no levee reinforcement), documenting levee patrol as local obligation in Phase 2 ($500K), and reducing Phase 3 levee-access debris to $150K contingent on BOTH Corps assistance denial AND RIP enrollment verification. The $4.93M reserve ($3.08M above minimum) buffers federal reimbursement uncertainty, shifting crest forecasts, potential PL 84-99 clawback, and unknown debris volumes. State resources (National Guard, DOT pumps, state sandbag stock, barrier contract) are provided separately per D7.

scenario.narrative: The $18.5M state flood-fight fund approved by the Executive Council under Iowa Code 29C.6 must cover Category B protective measures and Category A debris removal for eight proclaimed counties. County requests total $25.55M, exceeding the $16.65M available after the mandatory 10% reserve. Fiscal capacity analysis (D6) shows four counties — Louisa ($2.55M gap, 6 days cash), Cedar ($600K gap, 10 days cash), Bremer (small reserves, early crest Oct 14-15), Benton (small reserves, early crest Oct 15-16) — cannot front costs or have minimal reserves with early crest windows. Four counties — Black Hawk ($14.5M reserves), Linn ($31M), Johnson ($22M), Muscatine ($4.8M) — have strong reserves and can front most costs. This proposal fully funds the four vulnerable counties ($7.75M in Category B) and allocates the remaining $8.9M to the four stronger counties proportional to protective-measure needs, with debris advances restricted to those with demonstrated fiscal gaps. State resources (National Guard, DOT pumps, state sandbag stock, barrier contract) are provided separately per D7 and not charged to this fund.

ledger_changes.narrative: The $18.5M state flood-fight fund approved by the Executive Council under Iowa Code 29C.6 must cover Category B protective measures and Category A debris removal for eight proclaimed counties. County requests total $25.55M, exceeding the $16.65M available after the mandatory 10% reserve. Fiscal capacity analysis (D6) shows four counties — Louisa ($2.55M gap, 6 days cash), Cedar ($600K gap, 10 days cash), Bremer (small reserves, early crest Oct 14-15), Benton (small reserves, early crest Oct 15-16) — cannot front costs or have minimal reserves with early crest windows. Four counties — Black Hawk ($14.5M reserves), Linn ($31M), Johnson ($22M), Muscatine ($4.8M) — have strong reserves and can front most costs. This proposal fully funds the four vulnerable counties ($6.35M with Louisa restructured) and allocates $7.97M to the four stronger counties (~54% of Category B requests), with Category A debris advances restricted to $50K tokens for critical access routes only ($200K total). Louisa County's PL 84-99 duplication risk is mitigated by prioritizing water plant protection in Phase 1 ($750K, no levee reinforcement), documenting levee patrol as local obligation in Phase 2 ($500K), and flagging Phase 3 levee-access debris ($550K) as contingent on Corps assistance status and RIP enrollment verification. The $4.18M reserve ($2.33M above minimum) buffers federal reimbursement uncertainty, shifting crest forecasts, potential PL 84-99 clawback, and unknown debris volumes. State resources (National Guard, DOT pumps, state sandbag stock, barrier contract) are provided separately per D7

## Public Law-84-99

# Public Law 84-99

PL-84-99: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers provides emergency assistance to state and local governments before, during, and after flood events under Public Law 84-99. Funded through the Flood Control and Coastal Emergencies appropriation, our services include technical expertise and direct support for flooding, coastal storms, hurricanes, and earthquake-related flood risks. Assistance is available upon state request and supplements existing local resources and National Guard capabilities.

Section 5 of the Flood Control Act of 1941, as amended, (33 U.S.C. 701n), commonly and hereinafter referred to as “Public Law 84-99” authorizes the Corps to undertake certain emergency management activities. These activities may include the strengthening, raising, extending, realigning, or other modification thereof as may be necessary in the discretion of the Chief of Engineers for the adequate functioning of the work for flood control and subject to the condition that the Chief of Engineers may include modifications to [...] # Subpart C—Emergency Operations

§ 203.31

General.

(a) Emergency operations assistance under Public Law 84-99 is intended to supplement the efforts of responsible State, Tribal, and local interests. Assistance is limited to temporary activities and measures necessary to meet the immediate threat and to preserve life and property. Assistance  ( printed page 68399)  may include Corps assumption of control over the management and coordination of emergency operations; however, legal liability remains with the responsible State, Tribal, or local interests. results.title: DVIDS - News - Understanding Public Law 84-99 Rehabilitation program
results.content:
“PL 84-99 is the foundation of our emergency response efforts,” said Sarah Jones, Chief of Emergency Management at the USACE Rock Island District. “It allows us to provide both technical expertise and direct assistance, supplementing the work already being done by Tribal, state and local authorities.”   
   
 Under the authority of PL 84-99, an eligible Flood Risk Management System (FRMS) – such as a local levee district or a drainage authority – may receive rehabilitation assistance if it is damaged during a flood event. All systems considered eligible for PL 84-99 rehabilitation assistance must be active in the Rehabilitation and Inspection Program before the flood event occurs. [...] USACE determines if a levee remains eligible for PL 84-99 rehabilitation assistance through recurring levee inspections. These inspections use a standard checklist to identify specific items to be fixed during routine, preventative maintenance and provide an opportunity for proactive collaboration prior to flood events. [...] A subset of the checklist items which are deemed critical to the performance of a FRMS during high water must be considered in at least Minimally Acceptable condition for continued eligibility. Levee inspection reports performed by USACE are stored online in the National Levee Database ( The National Levee Database captures all known levee systems nationwide, allowing the public, agencies, and decision makers to assess risk, focus priorities, support preparedness and promote collaboration.  
   
 In addition to the cost benefits of the program, USACE also provides a multi-disciplined team of engineers, scientists, and technical experts to design eligible projects utilizing over 100 years of institutional expertise constructing similar projects in the same watershed.

results.title: Rock Island District > Missions > Flood Risk Management > Levee Safety Program > Public Law 84-99 Program
results.content:
Districts work closely with respective project sponsors if a levee system  receives an overall rating of unacceptable to explain the deficiencies and help devise a plan to correct the deficiencies. The sponsor is placed in an inactive status until the corrections are made. The levee system remains eligible for flood fighting assistance, but not federal rehabilitation assistance. The respective Corps district will also notify the appropriate Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) region and state and local emergency management agencies of the inspection results.

Deliver vital engineering solutions, in collaboration with our partners, to secure our Nation, energize our economy, and reduce disaster risk. [...] Beginning in 2006, all Rock Island District Public Law 84-99 Levee sponsors have been given a copy of the Levee Owner’s Manual that documents procedures for inspection and continued participation in the Public Law 84-99 program.

Ratings given to a levee system as a result of Corps inspections, sometimes referred to as continuing eligibility inspections (CEI), are used to determine if a project is “active” in the Corps' Rehabilitation and Inspection Program (RIP).  Active levee systems are eligible for federal rehabilitation funds (authorized by Public Law 84-99) for damages as a result of a flood event. A levee system must maintain an Acceptable or Minimally Acceptable rating on 18 line items to remain active. ## Note

 Note: Information on this page serves as a general guideline regarding repairs to flood-damaged levee systems and flood damage reduction projects within the jurisdiction of the Corps’ Portland District following a flood event. This information does not include all the details concerning the review and approval process for repairs to levees and flood damage reduction projects and these guidelines are not a guarantee of federal assistance. 

[](https://www.nwp.usace.army.mil/Missions/Flood-Risk-Management/Levees/PL84-99)

## Levee Rehabilitation & Inspection Program (Public Law 84-99)

![Image 2: Image of levee construction related to PL 84-99](https://www.nwp.usace.army.mil/portals/24/siteimages/Water/Levees/20121010-A-OH748-003.jpg)Enrollment in the Rehabilitation & Inspection Program under Public Law 84-99 (PL 84-99) provides reimbursement for specific damages to levees that result from high-water events.

The program is a partnered solution to flood damage similar to hazard insurance that you may have on your house. The levee sponsor enrolls in the program and provides levee maintenance to a standard level that is acceptable to the Corps. This maintenance and proper operation of the levee prevents routine damages and reduces the possibility of levee failure. In the case of severe flood-related levee damage to a properly maintained levee, the Corps provides post-damage assistance.

Levees are either federally constructed and enhanced in cooperation with a local sponsor then turned over to the local sponsor to own and operate, or are non-federally constructed or enhanced and owned and operated by a local sponsor. Federally designed and constructed levees are enrolled at the end of construction; non-federally constructed levees have to apply and be accepted into the Public Law 84-99 program. In Portland District, the sponsor is responsible for the operation, maintenance, repair and replacement of the levee in both cases.

Responsibilities of the sponsor and the Corps are set out in the programmatic guidance documents. Beginning in 2006, all Portland District Public Law 84-99 Levee sponsors received a copy of the [Levee Owner’s Manual](http://www.mvr.usace.army.mil/Portals/48/docs/EC/LSP/LeveeOwnersManual.pdf)that documents procedures for inspection and continued participation in the Public Law 84-99 program.

[](https://www.nwp.usace.army.mil/Missions/Flood-Risk-Management/Levees/PL84-99)

## Program eligibility

Levee systems that are eligible for rehabilitation assistance under Public Law (P.L.) 84-99 following flood or storm damage include those federally authorized, operated and maintained by a non-federal sponsor or non-federally built, operated and maintained by a non-federal sponsor. These levees remain eligible if operated and maintained to acceptable or minimally acceptable standards.

Federal government policy regarding repairs to levee systems and flood control projects damaged by floods is as follows:

*   Federally constructed or enhanced; locally maintained systems (in PL 84-99 program): Will be repaired by the federal government at 100 percent federal cost. Pending letter of request by maintaining authority and funding by Congress.
*   Non-federally constructed; locally maintained systems (in PL 84-99 program): Will be repaired by the federal government at 80 percent federal/20 percent local cost share. Pending letter of request by maintaining authority and funding by Congress.
*   Systems NOT in the PL 84-99 program; Federally or non-federally constructed or enhanced; locally maintained systems: Will NOT be repaired by the federal government.  
_*Note: Repairs can only be made to pre-event conditions. No improvements or enhancements with federal funding are authorized._

  

[](https://www.nwp.usace.army.mil/Missions/Flood-Risk-Management/Levees/PL84-99)

## Ratings and inspections

Levee systems and/or flood control projects are authorized for repairs if damaged by a flood event when the levee system is within the Corps' PL 84-99 program.Ratings given to a levee system as a result of Corps inspections (sometimes referred to as continuing eligibility inspections) are used to determine if a project is **“active”** in the Corps' Rehabilitation and Inspection Program.

To be included in the PL 84-99 program, a levee system or flood control project must be routinely inspected by the Corps of Engineers and found to meet Corps of Engineers construction standards and to be maintained in a fashion that does not deter from its structural integrity.A levee system must maintain an**Acceptable**or**Minimally Acceptable**rating on 18 line items to remain active.

Examples of conditions that will lessen the integrity of a levee system and/or flood control project and may result in a Corps determination that the levee system/flood control project does not meet Corps standards: burrow holes (mammal or man-made), tree growth (roots degrade structure; tree weight causes undue stress), erosion, any other condition determined to be a detriment to the structure.

Portland District works closely with project sponsors if a levee system receives an overall rating of unacceptable to explain the deficiencies and help devise a plan to correct the deficiencies. The sponsor is placed in an inactive status until the corrections are made. The levee system remains eligible for flood fighting assistance, but not federal rehabilitation assistance. The Corps also will notify the appropriate Federal Emergency Management Agency region and state and local emergency management agencies of the inspection results.

**Criteria:**On March 21, 2014, the Corps released interim policy guidance for determining eligibility status of Flood Damage Reduction Systems in the Public Law (PL) 84-99 Rehabilitation and Inspection Program. This interim policy changes the way PL 84-99 Rehabilitation and Inspection Program eligibility is determined for flood damage reduction systems.

Eighteen line items in the USACE Flood Damage Reduction System inspection report have been identified as the criteria that will be used to determine P.L. 84-99 eligibility. These line items are referred to as the interim eligibility inspection criteria. Any line item rating of Unacceptable “U” on any one of the eighteen inspection items will generate an inactive status in the P.L. 84-99 Rehabilitation and Inspection Program. Line item ratings of Minimally Acceptable “M”, Acceptable “A”, or Not Applicable “N/A” on all the eighteen line items will generate an active status in PL 84-99.

The maintaining authority will be notified of failure to meet Corps standards and be provided ample time to correct deficiencies. If deficiencies are not corrected, the levee system/flood control project will be removed from the PL 84-99 program and become ineligible for federally assisted repairs if damages are incurred due to a flood event.

[](https://www.nwp.usace.army.mil/Missions/Flood-Risk-Management/Levees/PL84-99)

## System-Wide Improvement Framework (SWIF)

The Corps now offers non-federal sponsors a process through the System-Wide Improvement Framework to remain temporarily eligible for P.L. 84-99 assistance while they correct unacceptable operation and maintenance deficiencies as part of a broader, system-wide improvement to their levee systems. Submitting a system-wide improvement framework plan is a two-step process. A Letter of Intent is submitted followed by submission of a SWIF plan. The applicant has up to two years to develop the plan.

A SWIF provides committed sponsors the opportunity to transition their levees over time to Corps standards. By using a SWIF, sponsors can prioritize deficiencies to address the highest risk first to achieve system-wide risk reduction.

In preparing the requirements for a SWIF, the Corps recognized that sponsors may engage at the federal, state, and local levels to address complex levee system issues in a more long-term, comprehensive approach to identify solutions that optimize resources; prioritize improvements and corrective actions based on risk; and coordinate overlapping or competing programs and requirements.

Examples of situations where a SWIF is appropriate are when a longer-term, holistic approach may be necessary to address multiple engineering deficiencies AND operation and maintenance deficiencies; when broader improvements involve multiple levee segments/systems; or when additional time and coordination are needed to consider complex, endangered species habitat or Native American concerns while meeting requirements for levee safety.

**Considerations prior to submitting a SWIF:**

*   May include corrective action for overarching operation and maintenance deficiencies, for example, a system-wide culvert replacement.
*   Is not intended for correction only of individual operation and maintenance deficiencies, for example, a single culvert replacement.
*   Is not a process for acceptance into the P.L. 84-99 program.
*   May include a vegetation variance request.
*   Recognizes regional differences.
*   Must be closely synchronized to align with other Corps levee policies.

[](https://www.nwp.usace.army.mil/Missions/Flood-Risk-Management/Levees/PL84-99)

Background 

USACE also has authority under PL 84-99, Flood Control and Coastal Emergencies (FCCE) (33 U.S.C. 701n) (69 Stat. 186) for emergency management activities. Under PL 84-99, the Chief of Engineers, acting for the Secretary of the Army, is authorized to undertake activities including disaster preparedness, Advance Measures, emergency operations (Flood Response and Post Flood Response), rehabilitation of flood control works threatened or destroyed by flood, protection or repair of federally authorized shore protective works threatened or damaged by coastal storm, and provisions of emergency water due to drought or contaminated source. • Preparedness: The Flood Control and Coastal Emergency Act establishes an emergency fund for preparedness for emergency response to natural disasters; for flood fighting and rescue operations; for rehabilitation of flood control and hurricane protection structures. Funding for USACE emergency response under this authority is provided by Congress through the annual Energy and Water Development Appropriation Act. Disaster preparedness activities include coordination, planning, training and conduct of response exercises with local, state and federal agencies. • Response Activities: PL 84-99 allows the Corps of Engineers to supplement State and local entities in flood fighting urban and other non-agricultural areas under certain conditions (Engineering Regulation 500-1-1 provides specific details). All flood fight efforts require a Project Cooperation Agreement (PCA) signed by the Public Sponsor and a requirement for the Sponsor to remove all flood fight material after the flood has receded. PL 84-99 also authorizes emergency water support and drought assistance in certain situations and allows for “advance measures” assistance to prevent or reduce flood damage conditions of imminent threat of unusual flooding. • Rehabilitation: Under the authority of PL 84-99, an eligible flood protection system can be rehabilitated if damaged by a flood event. The flood system would be restored to its pre-disaster status at no cost to the Federal system owner, and at 20% cost to the eligible non-Federal system owner. All systems considered eligible for PL 84-99 rehabilitation assistance have to be in the Rehabilitation and Inspection Program (RIP) prior to the flood event. Acceptable operation and maintenance by the public levee sponsor are verified by levee inspections conducted by the Corps on a regular basis. The Corps has the responsibility to coordinate levee repair issues with interested Federal, State, and local agencies following natural disaster events where flood control works are damaged.

PL 84-99 ADVANCED MEASURES – TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE (Class 520):

Overview: USACE is authorized to provide supplemental technical assistance prior to the event for Communities threatened with imminent flooding potential.  Assistance is provided to protect life and protection of public facilities/infrastructure.  Assistance requires HQUSACE approval.

-State Emergency Management Agency/Tribal letter requesting assistance required

-Evaluate flood threat to area

-Supplement data collection efforts

-Inspect existing Flood Control Works and identify problems

 -Provide engineering technical services

 -Provide information for local contingency/flood fight plans

PL 84-99 ADVANCED MEASURES – DIRECT ASSISTANCE (Class 510): [...] -Loaned supplies and equipment(Pumps, sandbags, and Innovative flood barriers) must be returned in the same condition as it was when lent, replaced in kind, or reimbursement made to USACE.

-Project economically feasible, reasonable, prudent and constructible before flood

-Project Cooperation Agreement (PCA) required

-Applicants/Locals are physically and fiscally responsible for removal of all temporary flood protection features at the end of the event

-Applicants must furnish all borrow, lands, rights, easements, and right-of-ways

-Applicants must make necessary relocations

-Hold harmless the U.S. Federal Government free from damages.

-Applicants must provide traffic control during construction

-Applicants must provide monitoring for levees and pumping operations. [...] Overview: This authority is initiated during a flood event, when river are forecasted, at, or

above flood stage as predicted by the National Weather Service.

-Assist or direct flood fight efforts

-Conduct field investigations/data collection

-Provide emergency flood fight supplies

-Initiate emergency contracting for construction of protective measures i.e. temporary levees

 Requirements:

-Supplemental to state/tribal/local government flood fight efforts

-Impacts to urban areas or critical public infrastructure only

-Temporary in nature and directed to the immediate threat

-Request from local/counties must be made to the State Emergency Management Office for their review and processing

-USACE must receive request from the State/Tribe to provide assistance
